issues.legal_issue: A later judicial decision finally determining ownership and the correct legal position constitutes definite information for reopening an assessment, and a valid reopening permits reassessment of the entire income that escaped assessment.
material_facts: The taxpayer had not included income from the mill in the original assessment while litigation over ownership was pending.
A later decision of the Privy Council finally determined that the vendor owned the mill and that the taxpayer had acquired it from him.
After that decision, the tax authority issued a reassessment notice for income from the mill.
The taxpayer had not disclosed the compromise under which he obtained release of the vendor’s sons’ claims to the mill and its income.
issues.conclusion: The later judicial decision constituted definite information and the reassessment proceedings were valid. Once validly reopened, the assessment began afresh and the tax authority had jurisdiction and a duty to assess the entire income that had escaped assessment for the year.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 34(1)(b) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, information includes information about the true state of the law conveyed by a relevant judicial decision. Income may have escaped assessment even if a return was filed, where assessable income was omitted or not taxed. Under section 34 read with section 22(2), valid reopening sets aside the prior underassessment and begins the assessment afresh, allowing the authority to assess the entire escaped income. The Court followed Maharaja Kumar Kamal Singh v. Commissioner of Income-tax and referred to Kamakhya Narain Singh’s case.

predicates.reassessment_proceeding: The tax authority initiated a proceeding to reassess income for a tax year.
predicates.later_judicial_decision_determines_relev: A later judicial decision finally determined rights or the legal position relevant to the income being assessed.
predicates.income_escaped_assessment: Income that was assessable for the year was omitted from assessment or was underassessed.

issues.definition: When a reassessment proceeding follows a judicial decision that finally determines relevant rights, and income escaped assessment, the reassessment is valid and may cover all escaped income.

issues.legal_issue: A lump-sum payment made to obtain release of claims to an income-producing asset and perfect title is capital expenditure, even if the claims also included profits, when the profit claim is ancillary and no share of profits is granted.
material_facts: The taxpayer paid a lump sum under a court-approved compromise to the vendor’s sons to obtain release of their claims to the mill and its profits.
The payment was made while litigation challenged the vendor’s title and the taxpayer’s ownership of the mill.
The compromise gave the taxpayer release of the sons’ claims; it did not give them a share in the taxpayer’s profits.
The Court found that the payment was made to perfect title to the mill and that the claim relating to profits was ancillary to the claim to the asset.
issues.conclusion: The entire lump-sum payment was capital expenditure, and no part of it could be deducted or set off against the mill income as business expenditure.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, expenditure to acquire or perfect title to a capital asset, remove a defect in title, or end a threat of litigation is capital rather than revenue expenditure. Expenditure to acquire a source of income is capital; a payment does not become partly revenue expenditure merely because income was considered in assessing the fairness of the settlement when the payment acquired the asset and the profit claim was ancillary. The Court applied the enduring-benefit reasoning in Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. and the distinction between acquiring the income-producing structure and earning income in Commissioner of Taxes v. Nchanga Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd.

rule.if: business_expense_deduction_claim and lump_sum_paid_to_release_asset_claims and payment_perfected_title_to_income_producing_asset and profit_claim_was_ancillary

predicates.business_expense_deduction_claim: The taxpayer claimed a payment as a deductible business expense against income from an asset.
predicates.lump_sum_paid_to_release_asset_claims: The taxpayer paid a lump sum to claimants in return for release of their claims to an asset.
predicates.payment_perfected_title_to_income_produc: The payment was made to perfect the taxpayer’s title to an asset that generated income.
predicates.profit_claim_was_ancillary: The claim relating to profits was ancillary to the claim to the asset, and the settlement did not grant the claimants a share in the taxpayer’s profits.

issues.definition: When a taxpayer claims a deduction for a lump-sum payment that releases claims to an income-producing asset, the payment perfected title, and the profit claim was ancillary, the entire payment is capital and not deductible as revenue expenditure.
